plants.temp_notes: Leaves freeze at about 32 F and plants die below ~25 F.
plants.light_notes: Pale tan/orange leaves suggest sun or cold stress.
plants.winter_summary: Cold-tender. Bring under cover before freezes.
plants.winter_triggers: Cover at 35 F, indoors/garage at 30 F or below.
plants.winter_steps:
Cover at 35 F or below (frost cloth/sheet draped to the ground over a frame; frost cloth buys roughly 6-8 F). Bring in or move into the garage at 30 F or in a multi-day freeze.
Water the day before a freeze (moist soil holds heat) but keep the plant dry the rest of winter; skip watering when it is below 40 F.
Cluster pots against a south/east wall under the roof, away from north wind, and pile mulch or leaves around the pots.
Stop nitrogen fertilizer now; new tender growth freezes first.
Keep pots in the covered porch; avoid winter rain.
plants.indoor_setup: Bright south window if brought in; water monthly.
plants.notes: Split from P-014 on October 21 2026: the old P-014 page covered three pots.
plants.water_notes: Soak when the mix is dry all the way through: every 2-3 weeks in summer and about once a month in winter. Keep water out of the center of the rosette. Mushy, translucent leaves mean too much water.
plants.soil_medium: Cactus mix with extra pumice or perlite: about half mineral. Use a pot with drainage holes.
plants.fertilizer: Low-nitrogen cactus or succulent fertilizer at half strength
plants.nutrients: Feed 2-3 times between April and August. None in cool weather. Pale, thin leaves point to low light; brown and orange leaves can be sun stress or cold.
plants.pests_watch:
Aloe mites (twisted, galled new growth)
Mealybugs and scale
Aloe rust and leaf spot
Root rot from wet, cold mix
plants.pest_steps:
Inspect the crown and leaf bases with a flashlight every few weeks.
Treat mealybugs and scale by dabbing them with 70% rubbing alcohol on a swab; repeat weekly until gone.
Keep water out of the crown, and keep the mix dry through cold weather.
If a stem turns soft or black, cut well above it with a clean blade and let the cut dry for a week before replanting.
Quarantine any new plant for 2 weeks.

scientific_name: Vitis sp. (possibly Vitis mustangensis or a hybrid)
id_basis: Rounded, shallowly lobed leaves with a woolly/felted underside and reddish tendril-bearing canes fit Vitis. Species cannot be told from leaves alone.

The October photos show the leaf undersides: pale, almost white and felted with hairs, which is the mark of the native mustang grape. The leaves are heart-shaped to shallowly lobed with blunt teeth, the bark shreds at the base, and the plant is vigorous in Texas heat. Most cultivated grapes have green, nearly hairless undersides.

to_photograph_add.note: Seen beside the boobie cactus (P-044) in an October photo: thick, hairy, pale-green leaves in a black pot. If you still have it, a photo would give it its own page.

requests_add.text: P-014 is now the biggest aloe (black pot with white gravel). The other two have new pages: the one in the teal pot, and the one in the black pot behind the prickly pear pad. Print labels for the two new pages (Labels page) and put each on its pot.
The speckled rosette in this pot now has its own page. If you want to keep them apart, it can go in its own small pot with gritty mix.
A close photo of the hand-written tag in this pot (only part of it showed), to settle which begonia it is.
Taste test: tear a leaf, touch it to your tongue and spit it out. Is it very sweet? (Stevia is.)
Press the yellow lowest leaf near its base: is it firm, or soft and smelly?
Look under a speckled leaf: are the black specks tiny insects (they move when nudged) or just dots?
Wipe one white-speckled leaf with a damp cloth: do the specks come off?
